question: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with a rapidly spreading leg wound, fever, and pain that is far out of proportion to the appearance of the overlying skin. Crepitus is palpable subcutaneously. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and priority management?

answers.text: Cellulitis; treat with oral antibiotics and wound care

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pain out of proportion and subcutaneous crepitus are red flags for a deep necrotising process, not simple cellulitis.

answers.text: Necrotising soft-tissue infection (NSTI); urgent surgical debridement with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. NSTI — including Fournier's gangrene and necrotising fasciitis — presents with pain disproportionate to visible signs and crepitus from gas-forming organisms. Source control (surgical debridement) is the priority; antibiotics alone will not salvage necrotic tissue.

answers.text: Deep vein thrombosis; start anticoagulation and perform Doppler ultrasound

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DVT does not cause crepitus or pain disproportionate to skin appearance; these features point to a necrotising infection.

answers.text: Gas gangrene (Clostridial myonecrosis); treat with penicillin alone and hyperbaric oxygen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While clostridial infection is in the differential, broad-spectrum antibiotics (not penicillin alone) plus urgent surgical debridement are the priority — not hyperbaric oxygen as the primary intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the clinical red flags of necrotising soft-tissue infections and the principle that surgical source control (debridement) takes priority over antibiotics alone.
Well done. Pain out of proportion to visible signs is the hallmark of NSTI; urgent surgical debridement is life-saving.
